source.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Connor Kissane; Robert Krzyzanowski; J. Bloom; Arthur Conmy; Neel Nanda

page_placements.theme: Attention heads and MoE experts are polysemantic at the unit level

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results about polysemantic attention heads, not individual neurons or MLP neurons. It therefore does not test any listed claim version, and it does not use the neuron claim as a tool or assumption.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions neuron polysemanticity in its introduction as prior work, but its own relevant experiments concern attention heads. The head results are recorded under fits_no_version; they do not establish results about neurons. SAE feature interpretability and circuit-analysis results are not rows because they do not measure a listed version or the neuron claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures polysemanticity of GPT-2 Small attention heads, using top SAE-attributed features and head ablations. No result concerns individual neurons (vision or MLP), their causes, architecture dependence, reinterpretation or measurement dependence. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited prior work in the introduction. The head results measure a related but different unit of analysis, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that attention output SAEs give sparse, faithful, interpretable decompositions and are a useful general interpretability tool (induction-head specialisation, IOI positional signal). From 14/144 plausibly monosemantic heads, they estimate about/over 90% of GPT-2 Small heads are polysemantic. They call the per-head method a rough heuristic, giving a lower bound on polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains sparse autoencoders on concatenated attention-head outputs and uses feature attribution and head ablation; it does not apply the original neuron measurements to neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The head classification relies on inspecting only the top ten SAE-attributed features per head and on subjective conceptual grouping; the authors note this may miss roles or misclassify heads.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2 Small, 14/144 attention heads were plausibly monosemantic. 81.9% were classed polysemantic, plus 2.7% bisemantic and 5.5% monosemantic with minor exceptions, based on the top 10 SAE-attributed features per head.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most attention heads in GPT-2 Small appear to have multiple unrelated roles.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating head 10.2 had the largest Layer-10 loss impact on both a digit-copying and a URL-completion synthetic dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single attention heads can contribute to unrelated behaviours.

fits_no_version.finding: The board-induction SAE feature is specific in high activation ranges but shows false positives at low activations. 'board' source tokens explain >99.9% of DFA variance above activation threshold 5 (App. E.2, E.3; similar for the 'Which' feature in App. G).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent polysemanticity of SAE features concentrates in low activation ranges (an activation-range dependence, but for SAE features, not neurons).

record.problems: The head-polysemanticity estimate is based on subjective human judgments and only the top ten SAE-attributed features per head; the authors caution that the procedure is not sufficient to establish monosemanticity. The two-head-ablation results are shown in figures without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Other SAE interpretability, feature-family, induction-head, and IOI-circuit findings do not test the listed neuron claims.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6 and 'discusses' classification is confirmed. No verdicts are given because no row bears on a neuron-level version. The 90% versus 81.9% discrepancy arises from category boundaries in Table 3, not from an extraction error.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Manually grouped each head's top ten SAE-attributed features by conceptual relatedness to assess head polysemanticity.
rows.measure: Fraction of heads classified as polysemantic
rows.note: The authors describe this as a lower bound: any unrelated top feature counted against monosemanticity, while related top features were only weak evidence for it. This is an attention-head result, not a neuron result.
rows.check: Value is correctly read from Table 3. However, 81.9% is only the 'polysemantic' category. Another 2.7% are 'plausibly bisemantic' and 5.5% are 'monosemantic with minor exception'. Only 14/144 (9.7%) are plausibly monosemantic, which is the basis for the authors' '~90%' or '>90%' figure. This is an attention-head unit, not a neuron, so it links to no version.
